Social and political changes in the 1980s and planning of the 1992 textbooks
The dominant thrust of China’s post-Mao education reforms was towards pursuit of the “four modernizations” through the reinstitution of radically elitist structures and selective mechanisms. Education, declared Deng Xiaoping, must “face modernization, the world and the future”. At the same time, however, reconfiguring the party’s legitimating narrative for the post-Mao era meant that facing up to the past – especially the recent past – could not be entirely avoided. The CCP Central Committee attempted to resolve lingering intra-party divisions in 1981, with a “Resolution on certain questions in the history of our party,” which publicly acknowledged “mistakes,” and assessed Mao’s legacy as “seven parts good and three parts bad” (Vickers & Zeng, 2017, p. 41).

But while striving to heal its own internal wounds, in the 1980s the CCP also faced the difficult task of restoring its legitimacy amongst non-Han minorities, whose culture, heritage and way of life had been subjected to particularly vicious attack from radical Maoists. In tandem with a more general relaxation of overt political indoctrination, the CCP loosened constraints on cultural (and religious) expression, emphasizing the principle of “equality among ethnic groups” (民族平等). The liberal wing of the new leadership under Hu Yaobang (1915–1989) believed that tolerance of minorities and recognition of their cultures could help rebuild their loyalty, which would eventually be cemented by the benefits of modernization (Bass, 1998; Hawkins, 1983).7 The introduction of policies and laws to strengthen protection for the cultural and religious rights of minorities was seen as an urgent priority (Bass, 1998). The Nationalities and Regional Autonomy Law (民族区域自治法), enacted in 1984, featured strengthened language on the protection of minorities’ “cultural autonomy”. Meanwhile, concerns to maintain control over “border areas” inhabited by minorities dictated preferential funding for schooling there, even while budgets were squeezed elsewhere (Vickers & Zeng, 2017, p. 40). This included support for bilingual provision in the more junior grades and, from 1985, provision of secondary schooling in “inland” regions for students from Tibet (内地西藏班), and later from Xinjiang (Chen, 2008).

Supporting the shift in official “minorities” policy, in 1988 Fei Xiaotong, the eminent ethnographer and vice-chair of the National People’s Congress, proposed a conception of Chinese nationhood characterized by a “pattern of diversity in unity” (多元一体格局). He expounded this in a talk delivered in Hong Kong, where Beijing was separately seeking to reassure nervous locals of its pluralist credentials. It was subsequently invoked as a guiding principle in official policy and in academic papers on ethnic relations. Although Fei stressed the “oneness” (一体) of the Chinese people and the core (核心) status of the Han, he emphasized China’s multi-ethnic origins and called for more research in this area (Fei, 2003).8

The 1988 draft Outline for History at junior secondary level, on the basis of which the 1992 textbooks were compiled, thus emerged out of a political climate marked by relative liberalism, and a conciliatory official line on Han-minority relations.9 For the first time, a small but fixed proportion of class hours (5%) was allotted specifically to the teaching of ethnic minority or local history, “the teaching of which had hitherto been sporadic” (Jones, 2005, p. 87). Overall, the Outline manifested a “demotion of theory” that Jones attributes in part to trends in professional historical research, which during the 1980s was increasingly open to influences from overseas (especially America). With the “straitjacket” of historical materialism loosening, attention to themes such as class struggle and peasant risings declined, with a greater focus instead on culture and the role of “Great Men” (ibid., p. 87). On the issue of ethnicity, the Outline states:

Our country is a unified multi-ethnic country wherein the Han are the majority. The history of our motherland is made by all ethnicities.10 History teaching needs not only to teach the history and contribution of the Han, but also those of minority ethnicities. The equality among ethnic groups, the safeguarding of national unity and inter-ethnic solidarity are the principles for dealing with ethnic issues in history teaching. The people of all ethnic groups developed close political, economic and cultural links throughout history. They not only engaged in friendly exchanges and contributed to the construction of the motherland together, but also together resisted class oppression and foreign aggression. (MOE, 1988, p. 3)

While emphasizing national unity, the 1988 syllabus thus also promoted a multi-ethnic narrative and stressed the principle of inter-ethnic equality.

According to RICT (2010, p. 291), this Outline was drafted mainly by PEP editors, though other scholars, including some from the Central College of Nationalities (中央民族学院) participated in an advisory capacity. One editor involved was Wang Hongzhi, later the leading chief editor of the 1992 history texts (Wang, 2000, p. 420). The representation of non-Han minority groups in school textbooks was a long-standing interest for Wang, which she attributed partly to an encounter earlier in the 1980s with Mongolian educators dissatisfied with textbook glorification of the Han general Yue Fei (岳飞, 1103–1142), traditionally regarded as “national hero” for his exploits resisting the Jurchen (女真族, forerunners of the Manchus) (ibid., p. 659).11 She claimed this had taught her that historical writing should “abandon the traditional bias of big (i.e. Han) nationalism and fully value the status and role of minority ethnicities in the historical development of the motherland,” which belonged equally to all members of China’s “great multi-ethnic family” (ibid.).

In her academic work, Wang projected the multi-ethnic reality of contemporary China backwards to the ancient past. In doing so, she cited as a chief inspiration her undergraduate teacher Jian Bozan (1898–1968) (Wang, 2000, pp. 218–9, 661), the eminent Uyghur Marxist who helped the CCP to develop a multi-ethnic narrative of China’s history (Leibold, 2007).12 In 1961, Jian had written:

… when we write Chinese history, we should be aware of not separating the history of the Han from the history of other ethnicities in China.… Do not treat these non-Han ethnic groups as foreign. Regardless of their relations with the central regime, we should acknowledge those ancient ethnic groups which inhabited modern Chinese territory as Chinese. (Jian, 1961)

Wang had been involved to varying degrees in compiling previous editions of PEP’s history textbooks since the late 1970s (RICT, 2010).13 As Jones notes, in these post-Mao texts “ethnic relations and national unity … featured more prominently” than previously, “presumably to counteract secessionist and anti-Chinese sentiment … exacerbated by Cultural Revolution excesses” (2005, p. 81). The curricular Outlines of the late 1970s included “eradicating ethnic chauvinism and localism” as a curricular objective, but this had disappeared by 1986. Wang explained that this was due to the steady diminution of “ethnic contradictions” since 1949, so that by the mid-1980s they had vanished, thus no longer warranting special mention (Wang, 2000, pp. 393–4, cited in Jones, 2005, p. 85). Nevertheless, textual content belied this confidence, with the definition of Chinese “national heroes” (民族英雄) reconfigured to embrace Genghis Khan and exclude Yue Fei, and prominence accorded to “the peaceful liberation of Tibet” (Jones, 2005, p. 85). Wang herself clearly continued to believe that the vision of a “multi-ethnic” China required vigorous promotion, as the content of the 1992 texts testifies.

The 1992 PEP texts: unity in diversity
Constructing a multi-ethnic vision of the Chinese past
The political climate in which these texts were actually drafted was rather different from that in which the 1988 Curricular Outline had been produced. The crackdown that ended the Student Movement of 1989 marked a drastic turn away from the relative liberalism of the late 1980s. The party ramped up calls for strengthening “patriotic education,” and introduced compulsory classes in modern and contemporary Chinese history at senior secondary level. The greater emphasis on Chinese history was also reflected in “interim” changes to the 1986 junior secondary Outline for history in 1990. However, when the 1988 draft Outline was formally promulgated (along with the new textbooks) in 1992, there were “few changes from the 1988 drafts” (Jones, 2005, p. 90; see below).

Notwithstanding her somewhat contradictory assertion that “ethnic contradictions” had been solved by the mid-1980s, Wang continued to aver that “the issue of nationality/ethnicity is a matter of great concern to me in the compilation of textbooks” (2000, p. 11). To ensure that texts were acceptable to all ethnicities, she declared, “the work of compiling textbooks must have the idea of a multi-ethnic country as its standpoint” (ibid.).

This agenda was reflected in the account of China’s origins in the 1992 textbooks. While continuing to use the term “tribe” (部落) to describe the first three Chinese dynasties – the Xia (about 2070–1600 BC), Shang (about 1600–1046 BC) and Zhou (1046–256 BC) – the 1992 textbooks for the first time also used the term “zu” (族, ethnicity) in relation to the Zhou (i.e. 周族) (PEP, 1992a, p. 27). This implied a vision of the Zhou as a distinct ethnic grouping or “nationality” in themselves, rather than as a “tribal” subset of a larger ethnicity. Wang’s later writing shows that she endorsed a multi-origins theory of Chinese nationhood (2000, pp. 220–1). She argued that the Xia dynasty was founded by the Huaxia (华夏), later regarded as predecessors of the Han, while the Shang originated amongst the “Eastern Barbarians” (东夷) and the Zhou amongst the “Western Barbarians” (西戎). This view differs from the traditional assumption that these three dynasties all belonged to the Huaxia, and thus were all ethnically “proto-Han”.

To further support this theory of multiple origins of the Han and China as a whole, Wang sought to draw attention to the presence of other ethnic groups around the periphery of the Xia, Shang and Zhou states. The maps used in 1992 to depict the territorial scope of these dynasties incorporated references to these ancient “minorities”. For example, the map of the Shang identified the Quanrong, Qiang, Di and Huaiyi as neighbouring ethnicities, highlighting the multi-ethnic nature of ancient China (PEP, 1992a, p. 23).

While 1980s texts had already projected the multi-ethnic reality of the contemporary PRC backwards in time, applying it to dynasties conventionally regarded as “Han” or proto-Han (such as the Qin, Tang and Ming), the 1992 edition took this one step further, defining neighbouring, competitor, “minority”-dominated dynasties or regimes as “Chinese”. In previous texts, such entities had been largely ignored – a neglect Wang interpreted as symptomatic of traditional Han-centrism. In 1992, the lesson on the Qin dynasty (221–207 BC) and its conflicts with the Hun (匈奴) thus not only mentioned the Hun in a section title (“The Rise of the Hun and the Construction of the Qin Great Wall”), but also featured a new paragraph introducing Hun culture. This discussed their customs and lifestyle, and was accompanied by the image of an equestrian statue of a Hun warrior and a map to illustrate their conflict with the Qin (PEP, 1992a, p. 72).14 Wang argued that the Qin, long hailed as the great unifiers, in fact only united part of Chinese territory – the Central Plain and the south. She stressed that the unification of the northern grasslands under the Hun was also an important “contribution to the unification of the motherland” (pp. 206, 222). This reflected Wang’s insistence that “the history of the motherland was co-created by all ethnic groups” (ibid., pp. 221–222) and that “all ethnic groups have contributed” to its “development”, especially in frontier regions (ibid., p. 54).

Similar treatment was accorded to the Khitan Liao (辽 907–1125), the Jin (金 1115–1234) dynasty of the Jurchen (女真), and (to a lesser extent) the Tangut (羌) Western Xia (西夏1038-1227), all likewise traditionally regarded as alien threats to the thoroughly Chinese states of the Central Plains (中原). The 1992 texts provided more extended coverage of the origins and development of these groups than previous textbooks.15 This enhanced attention to the domestic histories of non-Han societies reflected another of Wang’s maxims: “write the history of minority ethnic groups from their own perspectives rather than the perspective of the Han” (2000, pp. 204, 224).

The 1992 texts thus evinced a stronger and more consistent emphasis on the essentially multi-ethnic nature of “China,” giving more equal billing to the histories of Han and non-Han polities and cultures on what was now Chinese territory. This principle was explicitly stated, for example in this comment on the commissioning by the Mongol Yuan regime of official dynastic histories for each of the three dynasties that had previously governed its territories:

The Yuan government organised writing the ‘History of Liao’ [辽史], ‘History of Song’ [宋史] and ‘History of Jin’ [金史] and treated the Liao and Jin equally with the dynasty of the Han nationality [汉族王朝]. This rightly reflected the historical situation then. (PEP, 1992b, p. 133)

Economic development in the Liao, Western Xia and Jin states was also discussed along with that in the Han/Chinese Song Empire (ibid., pp. 123–149), whereas previously the domestic affairs of “minority” states had been almost entirely ignored.

The 1992 texts also covered non-Han regimes ignored in previous editions. These included the Western Liao (西辽), founded by Khitan who fled to what is now western China and central Asia after defeat by the Jurchen Jin (PEP, 1992b, p. 84). The Black Khan Dynasty (黑汉王朝), Western Uyghur (西州回鹘) and Dali (大理) regimes were also discussed for the first time as states co-existing with the Song. Wang observed that “minority” regimes had previously been featured only because of their links with dynasties of the Central Plain (2000, pp. 203–4). By contrast, the 1992 texts adopted the line that any state that had ever governed territory falling even partly within the present-day boundaries of China should be regarded as “Chinese.” Attempting to legitimate this view, the texts claimed (rather dubiously) that mainstream historians had always regarded the Western Liao as a “Chinese” dynasty similar to the Song, Liao and Western Xia (PEP, 1992b, p. 85).

The heightened attention accorded to “minorities” also extended to their “heroes,” many of whom were now hailed as “outstanding leaders”, “famous politicians”, “outstanding talents” and even “national heroes” (the ultimate accolade). Genghis Khan had already been installed in the pantheon of national heroism; in the 1992 edition, he was described as an “outstanding politician and militarist of the ethnic Mongolian group in our ancient national history” (ibid., p. 109). In his case and those of several other “minority” figures, the 1992 texts sought to enhance their exemplary status by recounting stories of their childhoods, emphasizing difficulties overcome on the path to glory – a common trope of traditional Confucian historiography. A biographical passage on the Jurchen leader Wanyan Aguda (完颜阿骨打) elaborated on his military skills, ambition and strategic nous, as well as his bravery in the face of insults from the ruling Khitan Liao emperor – all portrayed as contributing to his eventual defeat of the Liao (ibid., pp. 83–84). While military and political leaders predominated, the texts also devoted enhanced attention to artists, musicians, poets from “minority” ethnicities.16

The 1992 texts were substantially longer than previous editions, largely due to expanded discussion of cultural issues. Eighteen lessons dealt with cultural developments under various “ancient” dynasties, up from seven in 1986. This allowed for greater attention to the “minority” cultures. Previous editions had tended to discuss these in separate sections, implying their peripheral status, but the 1992 edition discussed cultural developments periodically, presenting Han and non-Han groups together. For instance, in the lesson on culture under the Sui and Tang dynasties, a passage on a famous Han medical expert (孙思邈) was followed by a sentence mentioning a Tibetan counterpart (元丹贡布) whose monograph had “laid the foundations for Tibetan medical science” (PEP, 1992b, p. 49).

Such innovations reflect attempts by the editorial team under Wang to challenge established notions of Han as civilized and “minorities” as backward. A number of passages stressed that cultural influence between the Han and “minority” groups was mutual rather than unidirectional – the Han could learn from “minorities,” too. A section on “Cultural Communication between the Han and the Huns” emphasized that “the Han people also learned a lot of things from the Hun,” providing several specific examples (PEP, 1992a, p. 107). An account of the introduction of polo during the Tang dynasty described the sport as having spread to China from Tibet (PEP, 1992b, p. 67).

Wang clearly saw her team as challenging Han chauvinist views and fostering instead a more inclusive, multi-ethnic vision of Chineseness. As we discuss below, other interpretations of this historiographical strategy also need to be considered. Nonetheless, the status accorded in these texts to “minority” societies, cultures and personalities was clearly enhanced. The same was also true of the coverage of conquest dynasties founded by “minority” ethnicities.

Legitimizing conquest dynasties – the case of the Yuan
In the early years of the PRC, attempts to construct a “multi-ethnic” vision of China did not mean any radical revision of established views of the major conquest dynasties, the Mongol Yuan and Manchu Qing. PEP texts of the 1950s and early 1960s still portrayed these as essentially “foreign” or “alien” regimes that inflicted destruction and suffering on the Han. The post-Mao adoption of a more pluralistic vision of China’s culture and historical origins dictated a more sympathetic portrayal of these dynasties. Here too, the trend towards a more inclusive, multicultural vision peaked with the 1992 texts. These accorded fulsome praise not only to Mongol and Manchu contributions to “national unification” (i.e., bringing Tibet, Mongolia and Xinjiang under central control), but also to their economic and social achievements. Sections on the Mongol period highlighted developments in agriculture, textile and porcelain industries, urban development, canal construction and foreign trade. Although one chapter dealt with the ethnically discriminatory policies of the Yuan,17 the overall depiction of Mongol rule was highly positive.

The traditional Han-centric narrative held that conquest dynasties were inevitably assimilated due to their cultural inferiority to the Han (Ho, 1998). Indeed, in the early 1990s, this was still the vision enshrined in textbooks on Kuomintang-governed Taiwan (Liu, Hung and Vickers 2005, p. 121). PEP’s 1992 texts did not entirely debunk this view, but they accorded heightened emphasis to the distinct governance strategies of the conquest dynasties. The lesson on Yuan rule pictures an official seal inscribed in the Phags-pa alphabet created by Basiba (Drogon Chogyal Phagpa, a Tibetan monk and Yuan official), highlighting the use of a script developed for writing both Chinese and Mongolian (PEP, 1992b, p. 119). Discussing Marco Polo’s sojourn in China, the lesson states that he understood Mongolian (and could therefore communicate with the ruling class), but does not mention whether he also knew Chinese (ibid., p. 121). There is thus implicit acknowledgement of the extent to which the Mongol rulers of the Yuan maintained their ethnic identity.

The texts play up the multi-ethnic identity of the Yuan in other ways. The dynasty’s capital (Yuan Da-du, on the site of present-day Beijing) is introduced with a passage describing the presence of Buddhist and Daoist temples, Islamic mosques and Christian churches, along with artists of various ethnicities (PEP, 1992b, p. 118). A lesson on cultural achievements stresses religious tolerance and the popularity of various faiths. Particularly emphasized is the Mongol rulers’ conversion to Tibetan Lamaism (ibid., p. 148). None of this chimes with the traditional master narrative of inevitable assimilation to the Han.

Instead, the portrayal of conquest dynasties (the later Manchu Qing as well as the Yuan) represents them as tolerant, cosmopolitan empires that governed their ethnically diverse subjects in accordance with their own cultural traditions. In her academic writings, Wang notes the existence of earlier Khitan prototypes for the Yuan and Qing approach to ruling Han and other ethnicities through separate legislative and administrative systems (2000, p. 195). Indeed, in her emphasis on the intrinsically multi-ethnic character of these dynasties rather than the teleology of assimilation, Wang’s position in some respects appears closer to that of the exponents of “New Qing History” than to traditionalist Han nationalism (Crossley, 1997; Elliott, 2001; Rawski, 1996).

Justifying the non-Han in inter-ethnic conflicts
The history of inter-ethnic conflict has always been controversial, as evinced by sometimes heated disputes over the designation of “national heroes”. Following her teacher Jian Bozan, Wang stressed the importance of applying “the Marxist principle of ‘equality among ethnic groups’” to the analysis of conflict. This meant challenging the traditional dichotomy of “righteous” Han and atavistic non-Han “invaders”. Wang recalled that post-1970s textbooks had taken an increasingly neutral stance on inter-ethnic conflict (2000, p. 184). In narrating the 11th-century conflict between the Khitan Liao and the Han/Chinese Northern Song, while previous textbooks portrayed the Khitan as invaders, from 1981 onwards all textbooks noted that the Northern Song attacked first. The 1992 edition took this principle of equality a step further. Discussing 16th-century conflict between the Mongols and the Ming, the text explained that the Ming emperor not only rejected a Mongol request for trade, but also killed the emissaries who delivered it. It portrays the Mongols as left with no choice but to resort to war, eventually winning a “peaceful market for trade at the Ming–Mongol borders” (PEP, 1992b, p. 173).

Elsewhere, the 1992 texts go further in justifying “minority” attacks on Han-dominated states. In accounts of Ming-Manchu conflict in the 17th century, previous texts portrayed the Manchus as aggressors, condemning their oppression of former Ming subjects in north-eastern China. The 1986 texts portrayed the Manchu rulers as enslaving former Ming subjects (who “fiercely resisted”), and the Qing as initiating attacks on the Ming (PEP, 1986, p. 67). However, the 1992 edition reverses the verdict, interpreting this conflict as the result of Manchu “resistance against the ethnic oppression of the Ming” (反抗明朝的民族压迫) (PEP, 1992b, pp. 173–174). It claims that the Ming bullied the Jurchen (later a core element of the Manchu coalition), forcibly extracting tribute and even “catching and killing” Jurchen people (ibid., p. 173). The Ming are thus cast as aggressors.

In the subsequent account of the Ming-Qing conflict, Manchu forces are praised for their wise strategy, while the Ming defeat is blamed on arrogance and incompetence. The Qing victory is hailed as “one of the famous battles in Chinese military history” (ibid., p. 175) – the most emphatic praise from an official history textbook for the conquest of China by a “minority” ethnicity. The fall of the Ming was conventionally regarded as a disaster for the Han, and a historical “wrong” that early Chinese nationalists fervently sought to rectify. This verdict thus underlines the lengths to which the 1992 editors were prepared – and licensed – to go in asserting a multi-cultural vision of China.

Political changes in the 1990s and textbook revisions
However, even while these texts were being prepared and trialed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the relatively liberal social and political climate out of which they had emerged was being transformed. The CCP interpreted the 1989 Student Movement as the outcome of a failure to “curb bourgeois liberalism and strengthen public morality,” and urgently sought to reinvigorate its legitimating narrative (Jones, 2005, p. 88). Against this background, patriotism (爱国主义) was given prime billing in a new campaign of thought reform. And from 1992, as a renewed push for market-oriented economic reform was launched, it became clear that the socialist ingredient of the official ideology would be further diluted (Vickers, 2009).

Despite ostensibly continuing to espouse socialism, the CCP increasingly stressed its patriotic credentials as “China’s past, present, and future saviour” not only from class enemies and foreign imperialists, but also from “China’s youth”, who had “tasted only the sweet fruits of modernization and not the hard years of bitter struggle, and were thus too easily led astray by the pernicious influences of decadent Western culture” (Jones, 2005, p. 88). Although patriotism had previously been one ingredient in the ideological mix, it was now “singled out as a spiritual crutch for the communist regime” (Zhao, 2004, p. 214). Following various directives on patriotic and moral education after the Tiananmen crackdown, a full-blown Patriotic Education campaign was signalled in a March 1991 letter by Party General Secretary Jiang Zemin. Jiang urged the use of education to “improve the self-esteem and confidence of Chinese people, especially Chinese youth, and prevent them being subservient to foreigners” (Jiang, 1991). Greater attention to the teaching of modern and contemporary Chinese history would enable students to understand China’s “national situation,”18 and thus acquire a “correct” understanding of the Party’s leading role (ibid.).

Two related ministerial directives followed in August 1991, mandating revisions to curricula and textbooks.19 New texts for senior high level were published – partly to support the teaching of new, compulsory classes in modern Chinese history – while primary and junior secondary texts were also revised to strengthen the “education of thought [思想教育] for loving the socialist motherland” (RICT, 2010, pp. 293–4, 420). Junior secondary teaching hours at Grade 2 (when modern and contemporary Chinese history were taught) were increased from 2 to 3 hours weekly. Ancient Chinese History, though not singled out in these directives, was also seen as important for reminding students of the “glorious 5,000 years of Chinese civilization,” thereby raising “national self-respect and self-confidence” to counter the influence of “western spiritual pollution” (ibid., pp. 450, 520). Reflecting the new ideological climate, Wang Hongzhi’s writings from the early 1990s also highlight the need to use history education to promote patriotism.20

The 1988 Curricular Outline and draft 1992 textbooks were revised several times to highlight the theme of patriotism (RICT, 2010, p. 419). In autumn 1989, when the texts were published in an “experimental” version, the Preface avowed “particular attention to education in national conditions in order to teach students to love the motherland, the CCP and socialist development, and ensure that they adhere to the Four Cardinal Principles” (ibid., p. 424). Revisions to the “experimental” version primarily involved modern and contemporary Chinese history, highlighting the themes of imperialist invasion and the united resistance of the Chinese people under CCP leadership (ibid., pp. 450, 456). Content relating to pre-modern periods was also revised, though to a lesser extent, in order to highlight the greatness of Chinese civilization (ibid., pp. 420, 450).21

With respect to the representation of minority ethnic groups, the formal edition of the 1992 textbooks featured several “touching stories of the patriotic activities of all ethnic groups” that had not featured in the experimental version. For example, the unit on the Qing (1644–1911) included a new passage praising the patriotism of the Panchen Lama in rejecting “the scheme of the British colonialists” for separating Tibet from China (PEP, 1992c, p. 3). Another passage reinstated from the 1981 texts having been deleted in 1986 recounted the tale of a Mongol people (土尔扈特 or Torghut) who overcame various difficulties to return to the motherland (the Qing) from the Volga region of Russia (PEP, 1992c, pp. 2–3). This episode was hailed as “a glorious chapter in the consolidation and development of our country as a multi-ethnic state”, earning the Torghut leader Ubashi (渥巴锡) “national hero” status (ibid.). Revisions invariably highlighted the patriotic behaviour of “minority” groups and their contribution to national unity. These changes also reflected rising concern over separatist sentiment among Tibetans and Uyghurs – concern that dictated greater emphasis on national unity and “inter-ethnic solidarity”.22 While these alterations did not fundamentally affect the core structure or content of the 1992 texts (as detailed above), unity and solidarity would become far more central themes in the subsequent edition.

Curriculum development in the 1990s was subject to contradictory pressures. The Patriotic Education campaign reached a climax in August 1994 with the issuance by the CCP Central Committee of an Outline for Conducting Patriotic Education. There was subsequently to be no let-up in the emphasis on promotion of patriotism as a core function of schooling (Zhao, 2004).23 Meanwhile, however, concerns over the capacity of schools to produce “human resources” capable of competing in the so-called knowledge economy prompted increased talk of the need for “quality education” (素质教育) to “comprehensively improve the quality of national citizens and their innovative abilities” (MOE, 1998). In April 1999, the central government mandated a sweeping curriculum reform to focus on cultivating abilities such as innovation, problem-solving and teamwork. The Ministry duly issued a new curriculum standard in 2001, which formed the basis for new textbooks that began to appear that same year. In drafting these texts, which remained in use until 2016, editors had to reconcile the conflicting goals of fostering more critical thinking (for the promotion of technological innovation) and inculcating decidedly uncritical patriotism.

The purpose of the revised texts was to promote patriotism and strengthen the "education of thought for loving the socialist motherland" in the aftermath of the 1989 Student Movement and the Tiananmen Square crackdown. The texts were revised several times to emphasize the theme of patriotism and to highlight the greatness of Chinese civilization. They also included several "touching stories of the patriotic deeds of minority ethnic groups" and emphasized the role of these groups in the "struggle for national independence and reunification." However, the texts also maintained a strong emphasis on the CCP's leading role in these struggles and its role in the modernization of China.

The 2001- 2 PEP history textbooks: unity above diversity
Although Wang Hongzhi remained the Director of the Editorial Committee for the 2001-2 History textbooks and contributed (with 11 other editors) to the volumes on Ancient China, by her own account she was by this time withdrawing from direct oversight of textbook compilation (Wang, 2000, pp. 18–9).24 Two new chief editors, Qi Jiaxiang and Ma Zhibing, took over.25

While the 1992 edition amalgamated the relatively liberal 1988 Curricular Outline and the post-1989 Patriotic Education campaign, the 2001-2 edition was more thoroughly in tune with the latter. This is evident even from the Table of Contents, which reflects a conventional narrative of the national past centred on a Chinese nation conceived in ethnocultural terms, rather than on a Marxist narrative of historical-materialist phases of development (from primitive communism through slave, feudal and bourgeois to socialist utopia).26

Enhanced ethnonationalism was reflected in a new emphasis on the Yellow Emperor (黄帝), a semi-mythical figure traditionally regarded as the ancestor of the Han people (see Chow, 1997). Described briefly in the 1992 texts as the “leader of a tribal alliance”, in 2001-2 he rated an entire lesson identifying him as “The Ancestor of the Huaxia [the proto-Han peoples of ancient China]” (PEP, 2001–2a, p. 12). A new section hailed the Yellow Emperor as the “first ancestor of [Chinese/human] civilization” (人文初祖), citing the inventions traditionally ascribed to him (including boats, wagons, the lunar calendar and medicine, etc.). He was represented as a symbol of Chineseness conceived in thoroughly primordialist and even biological terms.27

This ethno-nationalist perspective reflected the political and cultural currents of the 1990s, but what of the personal predilections of the new chief editors? A search on CNKI (中国知网) shows that Qi has published two papers related to the issue of ethnicity (1982, 2005) and Ma only one. None of these evince a strong espousal of the kind of multi-ethnic perspective promoted by Wang.28 They emphasize themes on national unity, interethnic solidarity and patriotism. In a writing entitled “Little seals with large functions” (小小印章管大用), Qi argues that a Han dynasty official seal found in Xinjiang in 1954 “shows that the ethnic Qiang group living in southern Xinjiang were already under [Chinese] governance” during the Han dynasty (1989, p. 150), and offers similar arguments relating to Tibet (188–9). The apparent views of Qi and Ma on “minorities” matters may help account for the shift in 2001-2 away from the previous emphasis on diversity and inter-ethnic “equality” – but it is also likely that the decision to appoint individuals with such backgrounds and ideological stances reflected the shifting priorities of the PEP’s political overseers.29

Ethnic pluralism nonetheless remained an important theme in 2001-2. Indeed, several passages dealing with non-Han ethnic groups were newly inserted. Following the lesson on inter-ethnic relations during the Tang (618–907), a new activity instructed students to survey their classmates to see if any possess “minority” backgrounds, exhorting them to learn about and respect “minority” customs and culture (PEP, 2001–2b, p. 27). A new section on inter-ethnic relations during the Qing Dynasty hailed the Manchu emperors’ tolerance of non-Han “minorities”,30 praising their policies as “pragmatic and far-sighted” (着识远见) and “benefiting the unity of the nation” (ibid., p. 114).

However, much material on the origins and customs of “minorities” was reinterpreted or expunged. The words “tribe” or “ethnicity” previously used to describe the first three dynasties (Xia, Shang and Zhou) were now replaced with the term “kingdom” (国), obscuring their diverse ethnic character and implying singular rather than plural ethnic origins for the Chinese nation. Many of the tribal names featured on an accompanying the map in the 1992 edition were removed from the same map in 2001.

The lesson on the Qin Dynasty, while still mentioning the conflict with the nomadic Huns or Xiong-nu (匈奴), omitted a section elaborating Xiong-nu culture and lifestyle, thus effectively reverting to their traditional portrayal as barbaric alien invaders. Under Wang’s successors, the attempt to incorporate such groups within an expansive, multi-ethnic conception of “Chineseness,” was superseded by a more Han-centric approach.31 As a result, coverage of the Liao, Western Xia and Jin was curtailed and simplified, with sections introducing their economic and social development alongside that of Song China pared down or eliminated.32 Passages on the Western Liao and several other regimes newly featured in the 1992 edition also disappeared. All these groups were now implicitly defined as non-Chinese, or at best as peripheral to the core, Han-centred national narrative.

Other passages dealing with “minority” culture and customs were also deleted. These included the Sarbi (鲜卑) folk song featured in a lesson on cultural developments during the Sarbi-ruled Northern Dynasty. The lessons detailing cultural life during the Northern and Southern Dynasties (南北朝, 420–589), when “minorities” and Han intermingled in the North, thus now entirely revolved around Han culture. Mention of the Tibetan medical expert featured in the 1992 chapter on Tang dynasty culture was deleted, while the passage on his Han counterpart was retained (PEP, 2001–2b, p. 35). Similarly, many minority heroes newly designated in 1992 were ejected from the national pantheon, or, as with the Jurchen leader Wanyan Aguda, mentioned only by name. One of the notable exceptions was Genghis Khan, whose “unifying” contribution was evidently considered too important to ignore. In discussion of Hun-Han relations before and during the Han Dynasty, the previous acknowledgement of mutual influence was removed, leaving the statement that “some Hun people learned farming from the Han” (ibid., p. 78), and implying a unidirectional, tutelary relationship in which the “barbarians” were subordinate.

While minorities’ cultural distinctiveness and claims to heroism were thus downplayed, episodes highlighting national unity and the immemorial origins of central rule in restive frontier regions (notably Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan) were accorded new emphasis. These included accounts of the Panchen Lama’s rebuff to the British and the Torghut Mongols’ epic trek back to the motherland. In one instance of the deployment of newly fashionable “active learning” in the service of uncritical patriotism, a new lesson required students to organize a historical quiz on the topic: “Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan have been Chinese territory since ancient times” (ibid., p. 132). The knowledge to be tested consisted largely of the dates when these regions came under the governance of the central regime. Notably absent from this lesson was any reference to the local inhabitants, their cultures, customs or histories unrelated to their ties to China.

Accounts of rule under the “minority” Yuan and Qing dynasties retained a positive gloss, but acknowledgement of their distinctively non-Han or ethnically discriminatory features was largely eliminated. Reference to the introduction of the Phags-pa script under the Yuan was removed, as was discussion of religious diversity in their capital of Da-du. Mention of the Mongol’s hierarchical classification of ethnic groups and the Manchu imposition of the queue (the long Manchu pigtail) for all males was also deleted. The effect of these changes was to dilute the “ethnic” character of these dynasties, making them appear more assimilated to mainstream “Han” culture.

Revisions also suggested growing reluctance to acknowledge past inter-ethnic antagonism, with accounts of Han-“minority” conflict significantly curtailed. An entire lesson devoted to the conflict between the Jurchen Jin and Southern Song was reduced to one brief section (PEP, 2001–2b, pp. 52–54). This entailed the removal of accounts of “heroic” Han resistance to the Jurchen attacks. Also deleted were the earlier accounts of conflict between the Mongols and the Ming, and of Ming responsibility for provoking the conflict with the Manchus that led to the dynasty’s collapse.

The emphasis on national unity in the 2001-2 edition was in itself nothing new – but unity was implicitly portrayed in terms rather different to those that had prevailed in 1992. Discussion and conclusion
As Duara argues, the 20th-century positioning of the nation as the master subject of historical writing in modern China came “with claims to territories, peoples and cultures of all of ‘its’ history” (1995, p. 28). And central to ongoing controversies amongst advocates of various “nation views” have been questions regarding “who exactly constituted the Chinese people” (Duara, 2013, p. 249). A key point of contention, intimately related to the vexed question of how the Han themselves were to be defined, concerns the place of non-Han groups in the narrative of the “Chinese” past (Leibold, 2007). Historiography thus became, and has remained, a battlefield over which rival visions of Chinese nationhood contend.

As this paper demonstrates, even within the highly controlled and centralized world of curriculum development in the contemporary PRC, clarity or consistency on these issues has proved elusive. Drafted on the basis of guidelines devised in conditions of relative openness, under an editor personally committed to a multi-ethnic vision of Chineseness, PEP’s 1992 textbooks featured significant recognition of the distinct cultures and histories of non-Han ethnicities. That attempt to promote national unity while acknowledging past diversity to some extent echoes the views of Gu Jiegang (1893–1980), one of the Republican era’s most influential champions of a multi-ethnic vision of China (see Leibold, 2007). In terms similar to those deployed by Wang Hongzhi, chief editor of the 1992 texts, Gu had argued that “the actual story of the frontier minorities” contribution to the [Chinese] minzu’s glorious past would foster the self-confidence and mutual understanding necessary for a truly unified body politic (ibid., p. 124). He strongly criticized Kuomintang attempts to deploy the myth of racial consanguinity to underpin claims to a unified Chinese territory encompassing “minority” regions.

It is important not to overstate the liberalism of the multi-ethnic vision adumbrated in the 1992 texts. These remained thoroughly infused with the teleology of national unification. Although the independent histories of “minority” groups were accorded unprecedented acknowledgement, they were still portrayed as streams flowing inevitably into the great river of China’s national story.33 And coverage of those histories was highly selective. In the “Ancient History” volumes, Tibet appeared only three times, on each occasion with the clear purpose of emphasizing its links with the Central Plain (e.g., during the Tang) or highlighting and legitimating central rule (during the Yuan and Qing). Despite their enhanced prominence, and Wang’s self-declared commitment to the principle of inter-ethnic equality, “minorities” remained marginal to the national narrative, and overwhelmingly portrayed as recipients of civilizational benefits bestowed by the more “advanced” Han.34

Nevertheless, the prominence accorded in 2001-2 to the Yellow Emperor, alongside the ditching of much acknowledgement of ethnic diversity, indicated a renewed intensification of precisely the kind of ethnocentric vision for which Gu Jiegang had attacked the Kuomintang many decades earlier. It is perhaps not coincidental that this turn coincided with attempts from the 1980s onwards to rehabilitate the Kuomintang itself, as the “new remembering” of China’s war with Japan stressed the united resistance to foreign aggression of all Chinese, irrespective of class or ideology (Coble, 2007; Mitter, 2013). That shift was linked not only to 1990s moves to place state-centred “patriotism” at the heart of the party’s legitimating ideology, but also to simultaneous attempts to reconcile “compatriots” in both Kuomintang-ruled Taiwan and Hong Kong to the “One China Principle” by stressing indissoluble bonds of (Han) blood and culture. That turn towards a significantly more Han-centric discourse of Chinese nationhood could only exacerbate a sense of marginalization amongst “minority” ethnic groups on the one hand, and arrogance and ignorance amongst the Han majority on the other. While school textbooks on their own cannot be blamed for this outcome, they have reflected and, arguably, contributed to a climate of heightened Han chauvinism and intolerance that is a key factor in the downward spiral of inter-ethnic relations seen in China over recent years.

What is the entry and exit of goods into the warehouse called?
The entry of goods into the warehouse is typically referred to as "receiving" or "inbound," while the exit of goods from the warehouse is typically referred to as "shipping" or "outbound."
Goods receipt notes vs Goods issue notes
Goods Receipt Note (GRN) and Goods Issue Note (GIN) are two important documents used in inventory and warehouse management. The main difference between them is that a GRN is used to record the inward movement of goods into the warehouse, while a GIN is used to record the outward movement of goods from the warehouse.

A GRN is generated when goods are received into the warehouse from a supplier or production department. It contains information such as the type and quantity of goods received, the supplier's name, date of receipt, and any other relevant details. It serves as a proof of delivery and helps in matching invoices with the goods received.

A GIN, on the other hand, is generated when goods are issued from the warehouse for internal use or delivery to a customer. It contains information such as the type and quantity of goods issued, the recipient's name, date of issue, and any other relevant details. It serves as a proof of dispatch and helps in tracking the movement of goods within the warehouse.
Shipments vs GIN
Shipments and GIN (Goods Issue Notes) are related to inventory and warehouse management.

Shipments refer to the physical process of delivering goods to customers or other locations, while GINs are the formal documentation that records the movement of goods out of the warehouse, such as when goods are issued to customers, sent to other warehouse locations, or used for production.

In other words, a shipment is the actual act of sending the goods out of the warehouse, while a GIN is the documentation that tracks the goods leaving the warehouse.
Bill of lading.
A bill of lading is a legal document used in shipping that acts as a contract of carriage between the shipper, carrier, and receiver of goods. It provides detailed information about the type, quantity, and destination of the goods being shipped, as well as the terms of the transportation agreement. The bill of lading also serves as a receipt of shipment when the goods are delivered to the specified destination.
Packing slips
A packing slip is a document that accompanies a shipment of goods and provides a list of the contents inside the package. It typically includes details such as the quantity, description, and weight of the items being shipped, as well as the destination address and any special instructions or notes. Packing slips are often used as a reference for the recipient to ensure they have received everything that was ordered, and to help with inventory management and tracking.
Packing slips vs Shipping labels
Packing slips and shipping labels are both used in the context of shipping and logistics, but they serve different purposes.

A packing slip is a document that lists the items included in a shipment, along with quantities, descriptions, and other details. It may also include information about the recipient, such as the shipping address, contact name, and phone number. Packing slips are typically included inside a package, along with the items being shipped, so that the recipient can verify the contents of the shipment.

A shipping label, on the other hand, is a label that is affixed to the outside of a package to identify the recipient and the destination. It typically includes the recipient's address, as well as any tracking numbers, barcodes, or other information that may be needed to track the shipment. Shipping labels are used to ensure that the package is delivered to the correct destination, and to facilitate tracking and logistics.

Bagaimana jika keterlibatan dan daya juang para anggota melemah dan menjadikan pergerakan ini prioritas ke sekian dalam hidupnya
Jika keterlibatan dan daya juang para anggota dalam pergerakan dakwah kampus melemah dan menjadikan pergerakan ini prioritas ke sekian dalam hidupnya, maka perlu dilakukan evaluasi terhadap kondisi internal dan eksternal pergerakan tersebut. Beberapa hal yang dapat dilakukan untuk mengatasi masalah ini adalah:

1. Refleksi diri dan introspeksi terhadap visi dan misi pergerakan dakwah kampus. Para anggota perlu mempertanyakan kembali alasan dan tujuan mereka bergabung dalam pergerakan ini. Apakah visi dan misi pergerakan masih relevan dengan kondisi dan kebutuhan masyarakat saat ini? Jika tidak, maka perlu dilakukan revisi dan pembenahan.
2. Membangun komunikasi yang efektif antara pimpinan dengan anggota. Pimpinan perlu memahami dan mendengarkan keluhan, ide, dan masukan dari anggota. Dengan adanya komunikasi yang baik, para anggota akan merasa dihargai dan diberikan peran yang sesuai dengan kapasitas dan kemampuan masing-masing.
3. Menyediakan program dan kegiatan yang menarik dan bermanfaat untuk anggota. Perlu disadari bahwa para anggota memiliki banyak aktivitas lain di luar pergerakan dakwah kampus. Oleh karena itu, dibutuhkan program dan kegiatan yang menarik dan bermanfaat agar para anggota merasa bahwa waktu dan tenaganya yang diinvestasikan di pergerakan dakwah kampus tidak sia-sia.
4. Membangun budaya solidaritas dan kebersamaan di antara anggota. Solidaritas dan kebersamaan yang kuat akan membuat para anggota merasa bahwa mereka menjadi bagian dari keluarga besar dan saling mendukung satu sama lain. Hal ini akan meningkatkan motivasi dan semangat para anggota dalam menjalankan tugasnya.
5. Membuat reward system yang efektif dan adil. Para anggota yang berkontribusi secara maksimal dalam pergerakan dakwah kampus perlu diberikan reward yang pantas dan adil. Hal ini akan memberikan motivasi dan pengakuan atas dedikasi dan kontribusi mereka.

Dalam melakukan evaluasi dan upaya perbaikan ini, perlu diingat bahwa pergerakan dakwah kampus tidak bisa diukur secara kuantitatif semata, melainkan juga harus dilihat secara kualitatif dalam hal nilai dan kebermanfaatan yang dihasilkan bagi masyarakat.

Dengan membagi target total NAFA ke dalam target individu bagi para relawan, NAFA dapat memotivasi para relawan untuk bekerja keras dan mencapai target mereka masing-masing. Hal ini juga dapat membantu NAFA dalam memonitor pencapaian target secara lebih terperinci dan tepat waktu.

Secara keseluruhan, penggunaan relawan atau aktivis dalam mencapai target pengumpulan dana ZISWAF NAFA dapat menjadi strategi yang efektif jika dilakukan dengan tepat dan dengan memperhatikan berbagai faktor yang memengaruhi keberhasilannya.

Bagaimana menurutmu?
Sebagai AI, saya tidak memiliki pandangan politik dan netral dalam hal ini. Namun, saya dapat memberikan beberapa hal yang perlu diperhatikan dalam mengambil positioning tersebut:

1. Pertimbangkan reputasi dan citra organisasi. Apakah dukungan pada partai tertentu akan mempengaruhi citra organisasi dan memberikan dampak negatif pada kredibilitas OLP di mata masyarakat?
2. Pertimbangkan nilai-nilai organisasi. Apakah dukungan pada partai tertentu sejalan dengan nilai-nilai dan tujuan organisasi OLP?
3. Pertimbangkan risiko yang mungkin timbul. Apakah ada risiko hukum atau etis yang mungkin timbul akibat dukungan pada partai tertentu?
4. Pertimbangkan potensi dampak positif bagi organisasi. Apakah dukungan pada partai tertentu dapat membuka peluang untuk mengembangkan jaringan dan memperluas pengaruh organisasi?

Dalam hal ini, perlu dipertimbangkan dengan matang apakah dukungan pada partai politik tertentu sejalan dengan tujuan dan nilai-nilai organisasi OLP. Selain itu, OLP perlu memastikan bahwa dukungan tersebut tidak melanggar hukum dan etika yang berlaku serta tidak mempengaruhi citra organisasi secara negatif. Jika diputuskan untuk memberikan dukungan, maka OLP dapat memanfaatkan potensi politikal digital marketing oleh para aktivis dan simpatisan PKS dari OLP untuk mencapai tujuan dukungan tersebut. Namun, OLP juga perlu memastikan bahwa dukungan tersebut tidak mengganggu keterlibatan dan keberhasilan organisasi dalam kegiatan dakwah kampus yang selama ini dijalankan.
Sudah diputuskan untuk memberikan dukungan, maka OLP dapat memanfaatkan potensi politikal digital marketing oleh para aktivis dan simpatisan PKS dari OLP untuk mencapai tujuan dukungan tersebut.
Baik, dalam hal ini OLP dapat memanfaatkan potensi politikal digital marketing yang dimiliki oleh para aktivis dan simpatisan PKS dari OLP untuk membantu mencapai tujuan dukungan tersebut. Ada beberapa langkah yang dapat dilakukan untuk memanfaatkan potensi ini:

1. Mengumpulkan data dan informasi: OLP dapat mengumpulkan data dan informasi tentang calon legislatif dari PKS yang akan didukung, seperti profil, visi, dan program kerjanya.

3. Membangun jejaring digital: OLP dapat membangun jejaring digital dengan para aktivis dan simpatisan PKS dari OLP yang memiliki pengaruh di media sosial dan mampu membantu mempromosikan konten dukungan tersebut.
4. Melakukan kampanye digital: OLP dapat melakukan kampanye digital untuk mengenalkan calon legislatif PKS tersebut pada masyarakat luas melalui media sosial, website, dan platform digital lainnya. Kampanye ini harus dilakukan secara strategis dan efektif agar dapat mencapai target audience yang sesuai.
5. Mengukur kinerja kampanye: OLP harus mengukur kinerja kampanye dukungan tersebut secara teratur dan melakukan evaluasi untuk meningkatkan kinerja kampanye di masa yang akan datang.

2. Manajer media sosial: bertanggung jawab untuk memperluas jangkauan kampanye melalui media sosial, mengelola konten, dan membangun hubungan dengan pengikut.
3. Ahli pemasaran digital: bertanggung jawab untuk merancang strategi pemasaran digital untuk mencapai target yang ditetapkan, termasuk pengembangan iklan online dan pengoptimalan mesin pencari.
4. Manajer acara: bertanggung jawab untuk merencanakan dan mengatur acara kampanye, termasuk pertemuan umum, konferensi pers, dan kampanye pemasaran.
5. Tim relawan: bertanggung jawab untuk merekrut dan mengorganisir relawan yang akan membantu kampanye, termasuk mengatur jadwal, menyebarluaskan materi kampanye, dan membangun hubungan dengan pemilih.
6. Staf administratif: bertanggung jawab untuk mengatur dokumen, menyelesaikan administrasi, dan mengelola anggaran.
7. Staf riset: bertanggung jawab untuk mengumpulkan dan menganalisis data pemilih, termasuk kebiasaan suara, perilaku pemilih, dan opini politik.

Dalam struktur ini, setiap posisi akan memiliki tanggung jawab dan tugas yang jelas dalam kampanye, sehingga dapat memaksimalkan efisiensi dan efektivitas tim dalam mendukung PKS.

GemPy是一个Python软件包，用于建立3D地质模型和进行地质建模。它提供了一个灵活的框架，使用户能够将地质数据与计算机模拟结合起来，以构建准确的地质模型。

具体来说，GemPy可以处理不同类型的地质数据，包括地质剖面、钻孔数据和地震数据，并使用这些数据来创建3D地质模型。它还提供了用于可视化地质模型、探索地质数据和分析模拟结果的工具。

GemPy使用了一些数值计算方法，例如有限元法和格点法，以模拟地质过程。它还支持使用Python编写自定义计算代码，以便进行高级地质模拟和定制分析。

总的来说，GemPy是一个功能强大、灵活且易于使用的工具，可用于各种地质应用领域，包括矿产资源勘探、水资源管理、环境监测和地震预测等。

当然，我会尽力回答你的问题，让我们开始吧！
GemPy的建模插值采用的是哪种方法？
GemPy使用的是“随机函数系列”（Random Function Series，RFS）方法进行建模插值。该方法是一种基于统计学的插值技术，利用随机函数和高斯过程来建立地质模型。

RFS方法可以处理具有多个属性（如地层厚度、矿物质含量等）和多种地质结构（如褶皱、断层、蚀变等）的复杂地质体系。它能够根据地质数据和先验知识生成具有物理可行性的连续地质模型。

在RFS方法中，GemPy使用了多个随机函数来表示地质属性，每个随机函数都有不同的空间相关性和方差。通过将多个随机函数组合起来，可以模拟出具有不同地质属性的地质单元。

GemPy中使用高斯过程来描述不确定性，这使得模型能够对地质数据中的噪声和不确定性进行建模。在这个过程中，GemPy还利用了核函数和最大似然估计来对高斯过程进行参数估计，以优化建模结果。

总的来说，RFS方法可以有效地处理复杂的地质数据，同时还能提供准确和可靠的建模结果。
难道GemPy不是使用的kriging插值嘛
GemPy在过去的版本中也使用了kriging插值方法，但是在最新的版本中，它采用了基于随机函数系列（RFS）的插值方法，而不是kriging插值方法。

虽然kriging插值在某些情况下可以提供准确的结果，但是它也有一些局限性，例如需要假设数据的空间相关性是稳定的，不能处理非线性关系，对噪声敏感等。相比之下，RFS方法可以更好地处理复杂的地质结构和多属性数据，并且能够对噪声和不确定性进行建模。

因此，GemPy选择采用RFS方法作为其主要的建模插值方法。然而，GemPy还提供了许多其他的插值和模拟方法，包括普通克里金插值、多点克里金插值、最小二乘法插值、有限元法和格点法等，以适应不同的地质建模需求。

要将克里金参数重置为默认值，请将参数`rescale=False`和`reset_kriging=True`传递给`set_interpolator()`函数。具体如下所示：
```python
gp.set_interpolator(geo_model, 
                    compile_theano=True, 
                    theano_optimizer='fast_compile', 
                    rescale=False, 
                    reset_kriging=True)

theano编译方式有哪几种
在Theano中，有几种不同的编译方式可供选择。以下是其中的一些：

1. Python 编译器：使用默认的 Python 解释器编译 Theano 模型。这种编译方式最简单，但也最慢。
2. C 编译器：使用 C 编译器将 Theano 模型编译成本地代码。这种编译方式比 Python 编译器快很多，但是需要正确配置 C 编译器。
3. CUDA 编译器：使用 NVIDIA 的 CUDA 编译器将 Theano 模型编译成 CUDA 代码。这种编译方式需要一个支持 CUDA 的 GPU，但是可以极大地提高训练速度。
4. OpenCL 编译器：使用 OpenCL 编译器将 Theano 模型编译成 OpenCL 代码。这种编译方式需要一个支持 OpenCL 的 GPU，但是可以在不同类型的 GPU 上运行。

要选择使用哪种编译方式，可以在 Theano 的配置文件中进行设置。默认情况下，Theano 会尝试自动检测可用的编译器并选择最快的一种。

How to transform the data that I get from database queries to the pydantic schemas in FastAPI?
To transform data from database queries to Pydantic schemas in FastAPI, you can follow these general steps:

1. Define your Pydantic model(s) that you want to use to represent the data you retrieve from the database.

For example, let's say you have a table in your database called `users`, and you want to retrieve data from this table and represent it using a Pydantic model called `User`. You can define the `User` model like this:
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str
```
2. Retrieve data from the database using your ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) tool of choice.

For example, using SQLAlchemy, you might write a query like this to retrieve all users from the database:
```python
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Table, Column, Integer, String, MetaData

engine = create_engine("postgresql://user:password@localhost/dbname")
metadata = MetaData()
users = Table('users', metadata,
    Column('id', Integer, primary_key=True),
    Column('name', String),
    Column('email', String),
)

query = users.select()
result = engine.execute(query)
```
3. Map the retrieved data to your Pydantic model.

You can use a list comprehension to create a list of `User` instances from the rows returned by the database query. You can also use the Pydantic model's `parse_obj` method to create a new `User` instance from a dictionary:
```python
users_list = [User(id=row.id, name=row.name, email=row.email) for row in result]
```
or
```python
users_list = [User.parse_obj(row) for row in result]
```
4. Return the mapped data as a response from your FastAPI endpoint.

For example, you might create a FastAPI endpoint like this:
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/users")
async def get_users():
    # retrieve data from database
    result = engine.execute(query)
    
    # map data to Pydantic models
    users_list = [User.parse_obj(row) for row in result]
    
    # return mapped data as response
    return {"users": users_list}
```
This endpoint will return a JSON response with a list of `User` instances, where each `User` instance corresponds to a row in the `users` table of your database.
Should I transform the data in the endpoints or in the services ?
It is generally recommended to perform data transformation in the services rather than in the endpoints in a FastAPI application. This approach helps to keep your endpoint code simple and focused on handling HTTP requests and responses, while delegating more complex data processing and manipulation to the services.

By performing data transformation in the services, you can encapsulate your business logic and data processing code, making it easier to test, reuse, and maintain. Additionally, if you have multiple endpoints that require similar data transformation logic, you can avoid code duplication by encapsulating that logic in a service method.

For example, you might have a service method called `get_user_by_id` that retrieves a user from the database by their ID and returns a Pydantic `User` model instance. This method might look something like this:
```python
from app.models import User
from app.db import get_user_by_id_from_db

async def get_user_by_id(user_id: int) -> User:
    user_dict = await get_user_by_id_from_db(user_id)
    return User.parse_obj(user_dict)
```
Note that the `get_user_by_id` method retrieves data from the database using an asynchronous method called `get_user_by_id_from_db`, and then transforms that data into a `User` model instance using the `parse_obj` method.

Then, in your endpoint code, you can simply call this service method to retrieve a user by their ID:
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from app.services import get_user_by_id

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def read_user(user_id: int):
    user = await get_user_by_id(user_id)
    if user is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="User not found")
    return user
```
By keeping the data transformation logic in the service method, the endpoint code remains simple and focused on handling HTTP requests and responses. This makes it easier to understand and test the code, and makes it more modular and reusable.

What is the best practice here ?
The best practice for specifying return types in FastAPI depends on the specific use case and the complexity of the response structure.

For simple endpoints that return a single object, specifying the return type as a Pydantic model is a good approach, as it can help ensure that the response data is validated and serialized correctly. For example:

```
For more complex endpoints that return a structured response, such as a list of objects or a response that includes metadata, defining a Pydantic model that represents the entire response structure can be a good approach, as it can help ensure that the response data is validated and serialized correctly, and make the code more readable and easier to understand. What should i Try QueuePool or StaticPool?
Whether to use `QueuePool` or `StaticPool` depends on your specific use case.

`QueuePool` is a good choice if you have a large number of clients that need to connect to the database simultaneously. It maintains a pool of connections that can be shared by multiple clients, and can automatically create new connections as needed. This can help reduce the overhead of connecting to the database, and can improve performance in high-traffic applications.

`StaticPool`, on the other hand, is better suited for applications with a smaller number of clients that connect to the database infrequently. It maintains a fixed number of connections that are allocated to clients as they connect to the database. This can help ensure that resources are not wasted on idle connections, and can help improve performance in low-traffic applications.

In general, if you expect a large number of clients to be connecting to your database simultaneously, `QueuePool` may be the better choice. If you expect a smaller number of clients to be connecting to the database, `StaticPool` may be more appropriate. However, it's always a good idea to test both options and see which one works best for your specific use case.

As a researcher at Lumere, my primary focus is on providing unbiased reviews of medical devices to healthcare professionals. Our goal is to help these professionals make informed decisions about the products they use in their practice, and to ensure that they have access to the most effective and efficient tools available.

To accomplish this, I conduct rigorous evaluations of medical devices using a variety of methods, including literature reviews, observational studies, and controlled clinical trials. I analyze the data from these studies and provide detailed reports on the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of the products in question.

I also work closely with healthcare professionals to understand their specific needs and preferences, and to tailor my evaluations and recommendations accordingly. I believe that by providing unbiased and evidence-based information, I can help healthcare professionals make better decisions about the products they use, and ultimately improve patient care.

It's important to note that as a researcher, my role is to provide unbiased, evidence-based information, and not to promote any specific product or manufacturer. My goal is to help healthcare professionals make the best decisions for their patients, not to influence them in any particular direction.

Manual:
The first sentence always contains the product name, what the product is, and what it is used for. ​
Always start the description with the name of the product profile. Use the full name exactly as it is.​
Describe what the product is in a couple of words (adjective, adjective noun) when not obvious from the name. This is often a reference to the group the product is in.​
What the product is used for should be derived from the approved indications/intended use and/or manufacturer literature.​
When restating the indications/intended use, be concise while not excluding critical information. ​
Do not just restate the exact wording of the indications/intended use from the filing or other source that will be displayed on the profile as these will be shown on the same tab as well.​
State the components, materials, ingredients, etc. that make up the product.​
A layperson that has never heard of this product should be able to visualize it in their head or "put a face to a name" with the product image.​
What other product(s) is this used in conjunction with and how? If the product is meant to be used along with another product, explain the purpose and the end goal.​

Here are some general rules for writing a product description. Learn from the given examples as a template.
General rules:
The full product name should be stated first in the description. Shortening a product name after this may be done in cases where the name is generously long and includes technical information (e.g. the product's diameter is included in the name).​

ALWAYS use an Oxford comma!​

Define non-obvious acronyms before using them in the description. An acronym should only be used when it is mentioned multiple times in the description or if it is mentioned in the description and another location in the profile (e.g. attributes tab).​

Don’t start every sentence in a description using the same word. It makes the description seem clunky and repetitive. Make sure the description flows; every sentence shouldn’t feature the same, formulaic structure.​

Be wary of marketing jargon when reading manufacturer literature or websites. Marketing jargon can loosely be defined as anything that promotes the use of the product but isn’t directly substantiated.​

Avoid technical specifications in the description unless it is absolutely necessary to explain a point.​

Spell out numbers less than but not including 10.​

Appropriately use “the” preceding the product name.​
Marketing jargon must be eliminated from profile descriptions.​

Here are some additional rules for writing product descriptions:

The first line should include the full name of the product as mentioned in the Name text box and a succinct intended use. 

When abbreviating a name or term, spell out at first mention, followed by the abbreviation in parentheses. (e.g. polyetheretherketone (PEEK)) 

Some commonly known acronyms that DO NOT need to be spelled out include: 

MRI: magnetic resonance imaging 

CT: computed tomography 

IV: intravenous 

DEHP: di(2-ethylhexyl)phthalate (this is the likely definition if the device is or contains a soft/pliable plastic, like blood bags, tubing, catheters, etc) 

OR: operating room 

LCD: liquid crystal display 

USB: universal serial bus 

LED: light-emitting diode 

Examples of acronymns/abbreviations that do need to be spelled out: 

polyetheretherketone is instead "PEEK"

expanded polytetrafluorethylene is instead "ePTFE"

polyvinylchloride is instead "PVC"

ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene is instead "UHMWPE"

Picture archiving communication system is instead "PACS"

Using numbers in description: Use numerals whenever the quantity is important

Spell out inches within text so as to not be confused with the word “in.” 

Use “non-sterile”. 

Use “follow-up”. 

If products are for use with another of the manufacturer’s products, say a guidewire, you would say “recommended for use with”, “intended for use with” or “compatible with” depending on the relationship. 

Use “MR compatible”, “MR conditional”, etc. 

Use X-ray not Xray

Use Luer (not luer). 

Use “cesarean delivery” instead of “cesarean section” or “C-section.” 

Use “emergency department” instead of “emergency room” or “ER.” 

Do not use periods for abbreviations within text. 

Use a comma in numbers over 9999
Example:
12,567 

Use one space after a period at the end of a sentence 

How to use colons and semi-colons:
The most common use for a colon is to introduce a list at the end of a sentence. Usually the listed items are separated by commas. 
Example:
The relief group needs many essential supplies: bottled water, cooking fuel, canned food, clothes, and blankets. 
If the listed items are phrases, separate each item with a semicolon. 
Example:
The relief group needs many essential supplies: purified water that can be trucked in; fuel for cooking, transportation, and heating; canned and boxed foods; and clothing of all sizes. 

Use the term "healthcare" as one word. 

Avoid inflated, hyped-up language. Be clear, straightforward with helpful information, and not copy that sounds like sales material. 

Be careful of making unsubstantiated marketing claims. Use “designed to” or “intended to”. 
Avoid contractions.

It is important to use precise and accurate language, avoid marketing jargon and unsubstantiated claims, and use proper punctuation and formatting to make the description easy to read and understand. Additionally, it is important to provide clear and helpful information about the product, including its intended use, size and dimensions, compatibility with other products, and any other relevant details. Overall, the goal is to provide clear and accurate information about the product that is easy for customers to understand and use.

Describe the product description manual
A product description manual is a document that outlines guidelines, rules, and instructions for writing product descriptions for a company or organization. This manual typically includes information on the tone, format, language, and style to be used in writing product descriptions, as well as any specific requirements for the type of information to be included. The goal of a product description manual is to ensure consistency, accuracy, and impartiality in the way products are described and marketed, and to provide clear guidance to those responsible for writing product descriptions. A well-crafted product description manual can help to improve the quality and effectiveness of product descriptions, enhance brand image, and increase customer trust and engagement.

--------
